purpose: Editorial recommendation metadata and inspected-source provenance for P47–P54, completing the drafting and revision family. Fields remain outside strict Commons frontmatter.

articles.title: Write Toward a Reader and an Effect
use_when: Conflicting advice leaves the writer unable to choose between revisions.
A draft tries to serve every possible audience and reading situation.
An intended emotional response remains too vague to guide choices.
mechanisms: Describing relevant starting knowledge and the situation in which the piece is read
Choosing an understanding, decision, or experience the work should make possible
Letting the intention guide prose while remaining provisional and distinct from observed reader responses
not_ideal_when: Exploratory writing needs room to discover its purpose before defining a reader.
The imagined reader would become a stereotype or a claim that actual responses are known.
example_user_queries: Every writing rule seems to pull my draft in a different direction.
I keep improving sentences without knowing what the piece should accomplish.
My audience description is too broad to guide a decision.
How much should I explain to someone new to this setting?
I want readers to feel uneasy but do not know which choices support that.
The opening tells our history before helping the visitor choose.
Can a story aim for mixed feelings rather than a clear lesson?
My purpose changed during drafting but the opening still promises something else.
How do I write for two audiences with incompatible needs?
Can I choose a reader without pretending I know how everyone will react?

sources.author: UNC Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Audience
sources.inspected_material: Audience matters, audience identification, and how much to explain: selection, organization, support, relevant knowledge, and the reading situation.
sources.supports: Using audience awareness to guide material, organization, and explanation.
sources.limits: The source concerns academic essays. No source example, biological claim, demographic generalization, or exercise is adopted. Its feedback procedures are not reproduced. The cooperative, revisions, and sisters’ story are invented. Practical reading situations, narrative effects, provisional intention, and imagined versus observed responses are editorial development. Stephen King’s ideal-reader book passage was not directly inspected.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed, self-contained prose comparisons make the changes in attribution, purpose, or process directly inspectable. No mechanical table, separate graphic, or interactive practice is needed.

articles.title: Separate Drafting from Editing
use_when: Repeated evaluation of an opening prevents the rest of the piece from developing.
The writer demands final wording before discovering what a passage is doing.
Polished local choices conceal an unresolved larger uncertainty.
goals: Flexible alternation between generation and judgment
mechanisms: Giving generation distinguishable attention when simultaneous evaluation blocks it
Using provisional language to expose alternatives and then returning to selection
Keeping factual gaps visible while retaining immediate revisions that help thinking
not_ideal_when: Local revision already helps the writer discover the next thought without repeated blockage.
Missing central evidence requires investigation rather than additional provisional prose.
example_user_queries: I polish the first paragraph every day and never reach the rest.
I cannot write the next sentence until the current one sounds finished.
How do I discover a scene without committing to every possibility?
My draft is rough; how do I know when to start judging it?
Do I have to finish the whole draft before correcting anything?
Revising a few lines helps me think; is that a bad habit?
I keep writing more possibilities instead of choosing among them.
Can I leave a research gap visible and continue drafting?
I need a perfect opening before I know what the piece is about.
How can I separate writing and judging without a strict timer or quota?

sources.title: Brainstorming

articles.title: Read Like a Writer
use_when: Reading produces admiration without a useful next choice for one’s own writing.
An admired passage becomes a universal rule without examining how it works.
Imitation reproduces objects or phrasing without the relationship that gives a technique its purpose.
goals: Craft possibilities grounded in observable choices
Careful distinctions among response, intention, and universal effect
mechanisms: Locating a specific change in the reader’s experience and connecting it to the text
Comparing an alternative to clarify a choice and its tradeoff
Testing the underlying relationship in a different passage while retaining context and limits
not_ideal_when: The reader wants pleasure, information, or companionship without a craft inquiry.
A claim about authorial intention or all readers would exceed what the passage establishes.
example_user_queries: I admire what I read but cannot use it to improve my own paragraphs.
How do I find what makes a passage feel reassuring?
I copied the surface of a scene and lost what made it work.
Does a technique in a great book mean I should always use it?
I can identify a device but not what it contributes.
How can I learn from a passage without imitating its wording?
A memorable line works only because of the pages before it.
Can an unsuccessful passage teach me anything about craft?
How do I separate my response from what the author intended?
I tried a technique I liked but it changes my character in the wrong way.

articles.title: Capture Material Before You Need It
use_when: A remembered impression no longer supplies the particulars a draft needs.
Notes lose the distinction between quotation, paraphrase, recollection, and interpretation.
A growing collection is difficult to retrieve or reconnect to sources.
mechanisms: Recording a concrete action or detail with enough context to understand it later
Keeping source locations and the status of borrowed wording attached to notes
Providing modest retrieval routes and a possible use while leaving interpretation provisional
not_ideal_when: Further collection would postpone drafting despite adequate material already being available.
An elaborate permanent archive would create more work than this project needs.
example_user_queries: I remember that a place was interesting but not what I actually saw.
My notes are full of impressions and contain no usable examples.
I saved a sentence and cannot remember whose words they are.
How do I keep quotations distinct from paraphrases when taking notes?
A useful fact has lost the page and edition where I found it.
I have hundreds of notes but cannot find the one I need.
What context should I preserve with an observation?
How do I record a possible interpretation without treating it as a fact?
I keep gathering more material instead of starting the piece.
Do I need a permanent notebook to collect useful writing material?

articles.title: Reverse-Outline the Draft
use_when: Rereading fluent sentences does not reveal the piece’s organizational problem.
Different passages repeat a contribution despite varied wording.
The opening promises work the body or conclusion does not deliver.
goals: Diagnosis before a choice of revision
mechanisms: Describing the existing units and their contributions rather than their intended content
Examining the condensed sequence for order, development, and mismatched promises
Returning to passages before deciding, using narrative and associative as well as argumentative functions
not_ideal_when: Condensation would erase distinctions the writer then treats as absent from the prose.
The outline would replace needed investigation or force an associative work into a claim-and-proof design.
example_user_queries: My draft feels wrong but I cannot locate the structural problem.
Every paragraph reads well and the whole still does not add up.
The ending answers a different question from the opening.
I keep summarizing what paragraphs should say rather than what they do.
My outline lists topics but does not show how the piece develops.
How do I tell repeated material from meaningful development?
Can I map a partial draft or a long work at different scales?
How can a reverse outline include emotional or associative passages?
Moving paragraphs around does not seem to supply the missing reasoning.
Two scenes have similar summaries but feel different when I read them.

sources.author: Rebecca Schoenike Nowacek, UW–Madison Writing Across the Curriculum archive
sources.title: Using a Reverse Outline to Revise

sources.supports: Making an existing draft’s organization visible for diagnosis rather than outlining only the intended work.

No full book-passage review is claimed.

articles.title: Revise from Structure to Sentences
use_when: Extensive sentence editing leaves the larger difficulty untouched.
Passages are repeatedly polished before being substantially changed or cut.
The writer cannot choose among revision needs with different consequences.
goals: Revision effort directed to consequential dependencies
Purpose and support aligned before extensive polish
mechanisms: Identifying decisions that determine the role of smaller choices
Reconsidering selection and development before protecting polished material
Tracing local difficulties back to larger uncertainties and returning to sentence work when its purpose is clearer
not_ideal_when: Purpose and structure already work and close editing is the appropriate next task.
A rigid order would prevent a local correction from clarifying a larger thought.
example_user_queries: I keep improving the sentences but the piece still does not work.
Which problem should I revise first?
I polished a section for hours and then cut it.
My opening promises something the evidence does not establish.
The draft changed direction and I do not know which passages still belong.
A sentence is hard to fix because I have not decided what I mean.
Do I need to rebuild the whole piece before correcting anything?
Some sections need more reporting while others are ready for editing.
How do I decide whether a beautiful background passage serves this essay?
How can I stop revising when there are still possible alternatives?

sources.author: UNC Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Revising Drafts
sources.inspected_material: The distinction between revising and editing/proofreading; purpose, focus, support, organization, and the discussion allowing movement between levels while preserving attention to the whole.
sources.supports: Prioritizing reconsideration of the work over extensive polish where larger changes remain necessary, without prescribing a strictly linear process.
sources.limits: No source example, author anecdote, quotation, exercise sequence, universal sentence rule, or empirical productivity claim is adopted. The bell essay, town, records, residents, and reading-room proposal are invented. Revision dependencies, local-to-larger diagnosis, differing section needs, and stopping criteria are editorial development. No named author’s book method was directly reviewed.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose comparisons preserve the context needed to assess revision priorities, audible clues, and reader responses. No mechanical table, separate graphic, or interactive practice is needed.

articles.title: Read Aloud to Hear the Draft
use_when: Familiar silent reading repeatedly overlooks omissions or unclear sequence.
A passage looks acceptable but its phrasing or pace is difficult to assess.
Repeated sentence shapes or emphasis need to be heard before deciding whether to retain them.
goals: Additional diagnostic attention to the written sequence
Purposeful choices about rhythm and repetition
Revision based on an inspected clue rather than automatic shortening
mechanisms: Encountering the words actually present rather than a silently corrected performance
Locating retention burdens, omissions, references, and repeated forms through sound
Distinguishing listening clues from their causes while considering access and intended medium
not_ideal_when: Listening is unavailable or unhelpful and another accessible form of attention fits better.
Audible fluency would be mistaken for factual verification or proof that the larger structure works.
example_user_queries: My draft looks clear but sounds awkward when I hear it.
I keep missing words I left out because I know what I meant.
How do I hear whether repetition is purposeful or monotonous?
I make a confusing sentence sound clear with pauses that are not on the page.
Does running out of breath mean I should split the sentence?
A pronoun becomes confusing when someone reads the paragraph to me.
Can text-to-speech help me notice problems without deciding the rhythm for me?
The spoken version works but the silent reader has different needs.
What should I do after stumbling over a sentence?
How can I check a passage when reading or hearing it aloud is not useful for me?

sources.title: Reading Aloud

articles.title: Seek Feedback Against the Intended Effect
use_when: General praise or criticism does not identify what happened during reading.
Readers propose incompatible fixes without locating the experience behind them.
The writer defends an intention rather than examining the response to the draft.
goals: Revisions assessed against a provisional purpose
Useful feedback without a requirement for consensus
mechanisms: Making specific requests suited to the draft and uncertainty without supplying the intended answer
Distinguishing reported understanding or response from a proposed remedy
Choosing relevant readers and using conflicting accounts, praise, and difficulties to inform owned revision decisions
not_ideal_when: The request would lead the reader to the answer or turn feedback into approval seeking.
One response would be treated as representative of all readers or as a substitute for verification.
example_user_queries: People say my draft looks good but I do not learn what to revise.
One reader wants a new opening and another wants the opposite.
How do I ask for feedback without telling people what they should understand?
A reader suggested an FAQ but I do not know what confused them.
Who should read a draft meant for newcomers?
I explain the missing information aloud before anyone reads the page.
What kind of feedback helps with a rough outline?
Readers disagree about an ambiguous ending; must I remove the ambiguity?
How do I take a problem seriously without accepting the reader’s proposed fix?
Can praise help me decide what to preserve during revision?
